notes.meaning: King Xerxes could not sleep that night, so he ordered the royal history books to be brought in and read to him. God quietly guided this sleepless night at the exact moment needed to protect His people. Even the restlessness of an emperor serves the Lord's hidden plans.

The reader happened to open the records to the entry telling how Mordecai had uncovered a plot by two royal guards to kill the king. God's hand led the servant to that exact page about Mordecai's past loyalty. An act of service that seemed forgotten was now brought to light at the perfect time.

The king asked what honor or reward had been given to Mordecai for saving his life, and his attendants told him nothing had been done. Persian rulers were famous for rewarding their helpers, so leaving Mordecai unrewarded was a major oversight. God allowed the reward to wait so it would arrive at the most crucial hour.

The king asked who was waiting in the palace court, just as Haman arrived early in the morning to ask permission to hang Mordecai. Haman was in a hurry because of his bitter hatred, while the king was eager to honor the very man Haman wanted dead. God was already turning the wicked man's evil plan back upon himself.

The royal servants told the king that Haman was waiting in the outer court, and the king ordered him brought into his bedchamber. Visitors had to wait outside until called, and Haman was eager to be summoned so early. God placed Haman in the royal presence at the exact second to hear the king's question.

The king asked Haman what should be done for a man the king truly delights to honor, without naming the person. Haman's extreme pride led him to assume that the king could only be thinking of him. His own boastful heart blinded him to what was really taking place.

Thinking only of himself, Haman suggested that the honored man wear a robe the king had personally worn and ride the king's own crested horse. He added that a noble prince should lead the horse through the city square, proclaiming the king's favor before everyone. Haman basically asked to be treated like the king himself for a day.

The king commanded Haman to hurry and carry out every single detail of this honor for Mordecai the Jew sitting at the palace gate. The ruler gave strict orders not to leave out anything Haman had proposed. In one moment, Haman's dream of praise was shattered by the very man he hated most.

Haman had no choice but to obey the king's command, dressing Mordecai in the royal robe and leading him on horseback through the city. He was forced to publicly shout the praises of the enemy he had planned to hang that very morning. God turned the pride of a wicked foe into public honor for His servant.

After the parade ended, Mordecai quietly went back to his normal duties at the palace gate, not puffed up by the praise. Haman, however, rushed home in deep humiliation with his head covered in grief. Covering the head was an ancient custom showing intense shame and sorrow.

Haman told his wife and advisers what had happened, and they warned him that his ruin had already begun. Because Mordecai was Jewish, they realized Haman could never win against him and would completely fall. Even these pagan counselors recognized that God watched over His people.

While they were still talking, the king's servants arrived to hurry Haman to the second feast Queen Esther had prepared. In Persian custom, messengers were sent to escort guests right when a banquet was ready. Haman was rushed away in deep dread, completely unprepared for the judgment waiting for him at the table.
